```{=html}
<div class="lx-interactive lx-cards" data-learn="news-lens" data-src="../assets/learn/data/n01-news-lens.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- fallback:start -->
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The seven questions</p>
<table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Question</th><th scope="col">Ask</th><th scope="col">The trap it catches</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td class="n">1. Scale</td><td>How big is it next to the whole?</td><td>A big-sounding number that is a small share, or a national figure read as a global one.</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">2. Time</td><td>Power or energy? Which hour, which year?</td><td>GW read as GWh, or a 2030 projection read as today's fact.</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">3. Physics</td><td>Do the units, losses and capacity factors make sense?</td><td>Nameplate treated as output, or a unit that cannot be right.</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">4. Who pays</td><td>Who pays, who benefits, who carries the risk?</td><td>Savings for one group that other customers end up paying for.</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">5. Boundary</td><td>What is counted, and what is left out?</td><td>A total that quietly leaves out part of the system.</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">6. Counterfactual</td><td>Compared with what?</td><td>A change measured against a baseline that would never have happened.</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">7. Uncertainty</td><td>How sure, says who, with what range?</td><td>One number from one party, with no range.</td></tr>
</tbody></table>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Story 1 · Data centers as a load · United States</p>
<p><strong>“U.S. data centers could use nearly 12% of the nation's electricity by 2030”</strong> <span class="lx-hint">Our paraphrase of how such reports get headlined.</span></p>
<p>A national-laboratory report estimates that data centers used <mark>192 TWh in 2024</mark>, or <mark>4.7% of U.S. electricity</mark>. Its Reference Case puts <mark>2030 use at 649 TWh</mark>, <mark>within a range of 521–843 TWh</mark>. Serving that load would take <mark>about 148 GW of grid connections</mark>. <mark>Cryptocurrency mining is not counted</mark>.</p>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>A researcher's notes on story 1</summary><ul>
<li><strong>192 TWh in 2024</strong> (Time): Energy over a whole year, not power. Spread over 8,760 hours it is about 22 GW of average demand.</li>
<li><strong>4.7% of U.S. electricity</strong> (Scale): A share of one country's use. Read it next to the whole, and never mix it with a global share.</li>
<li><strong>2030 use at 649 TWh</strong> (Time): A model's projection six years ahead, not a measurement: 2024 is the report's last historical year.</li>
<li><strong>within a range of 521–843 TWh</strong> (Uncertainty): The authors' own range: its top is 1.6 times its bottom. The IEA's early-2025 projection for 2030, about 430 TWh, sits below it (report, p. 10).</li>
<li><strong>about 148 GW of grid connections</strong> (Physics): Capacity, not energy: the report turns 649 TWh into GW by assuming connections are used at 50% on average.</li>
<li><strong>Cryptocurrency mining is not counted</strong> (Boundary): What counts as a data center is a choice; a study that includes mining reports a larger number.</li>
<li><strong>Left unanswered</strong> (Who pays): Who pays for the new lines and plants that serve large loads depends on each utility's tariff rules, and the story does not say. Upcoming: lesson A4 on large-load tariffs.</li>
<li><strong>A researcher's take</strong>: I accept the direction, strong growth in U.S. data-center use by 2030, but not the exact 11.8%. A new estimate built on lower chip shipments or lower server power would change my mind. Confidence: medium, since credible projections still differ by about 50%.</li></ul></details>
<p class="lx-hint">Source: <a href="https://www.energy.gov/documents/united-states-data-center-energy-usage-report-2025-update">LBNL, United States Data Center Energy Usage Report: 2025 Update, pp. 5, 8–10 (PDF)</a> (published 18 June 2026)</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Story 2 · Storage · United States</p>
<p><strong>“A record 15 GW of batteries joined the U.S. grid in 2025”</strong> <span class="lx-hint">Our paraphrase of how the data release was headlined.</span></p>
<p>Developers added <mark>a record 15 GW of battery storage</mark> in 2025, <mark>according to preliminary data</mark>. At the start of the year, <mark>18.2 GW had been planned</mark>. <mark>Solar led with 27.2 GW</mark> of <mark>53 GW in total</mark>. <mark>The count covers utility-scale plants of 1 MW and up</mark>.</p>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>A researcher's notes on story 2</summary><ul>
<li><strong>a record 15 GW of battery storage</strong> (Time): GW is power: how fast the batteries can deliver, not how much energy they hold. Energy in GWh needs the duration, which the story does not give.</li>
<li><strong>according to preliminary data</strong> (Uncertainty): Preliminary counts come from a monthly inventory and are revised when the final annual data arrive.</li>
<li><strong>18.2 GW had been planned</strong> (Uncertainty): Planned is not built: about 82% of the planned battery capacity arrived within the year (15 ÷ 18.2).</li>
<li><strong>Solar led with 27.2 GW</strong> (Physics): A GW of solar makes less energy in a year than a GW of a plant that runs most hours: compare capacity factors, not GW.</li>
<li><strong>53 GW in total</strong> (Scale): Big for one year. For scale, U.S. use averaged about 480 GW across 2025 (4.20 trillion kWh ÷ 8,760 h).</li>
<li><strong>The count covers utility-scale plants of 1 MW and up</strong> (Boundary): Home batteries and rooftop solar sit outside this count.</li>
<li><strong>Left unanswered</strong> (Who pays): Who pays for the batteries, and who earns from them, depends on market rules and contracts; the story does not say. Upcoming: lesson A2 on contracts and risk.</li>
<li><strong>A researcher's take</strong>: I accept that a record amount of battery power, about 15 GW, came online in 2025, as a preliminary count. Final annual data showing a much lower figure would change my mind. Confidence: high for the power; the energy stored cannot be known from this story.</li></ul></details>
<p class="lx-hint">Source: <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=67205">EIA, Today in Energy: 2025 additions, preliminary</a> (20 February 2026); <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=64586">EIA, Today in Energy: additions planned for 2025</a> (24 February 2025); <a href="https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/electricity-in-the-us-generation-capacity-and-sales.php">EIA, Energy Explained: utility-scale means 1 MW or more</a> (checked 2 November 2026); <a href="https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/use-of-electricity.php">EIA, Energy Explained: U.S. use 4.20 trillion kWh in 2025</a> (data for 2025); <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=51798">EIA, Today in Energy: battery duration = MWh ÷ MW</a> (25 March 2022)</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Story 3 · Reliability · Spain and Portugal</p>
<p><strong>“Renewables caused the Iberian blackout”</strong> <span class="lx-hint">Our paraphrase of a claim that circulated within a day; no single outlet is quoted.</span></p>
<p>At 12:33 local time on 28 April 2025, <mark>the power systems of Spain and Portugal</mark> collapsed. <mark>Within a day, posts and headlines named one cause</mark>: <mark>renewables</mark>. The European grid operators' expert panel found <mark>many interacting factors</mark>, including <mark>gaps in voltage and reactive-power control</mark>, oscillations, and generators disconnecting in a cascade.</p>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>A researcher's notes on story 3</summary><ul>
<li><strong>the power systems of Spain and Portugal</strong> (Scale): Two whole national systems went dark, not one plant or one city: that is why a formal investigation followed.</li>
<li><strong>Within a day, posts and headlines named one cause</strong> (Time): The claim came before the evidence: the expert panel's factual report took 158 days, its final report 326.</li>
<li><strong>renewables</strong> (Uncertainty): A single cause from early, partial information. Ask who says it and what data they had.</li>
<li><strong>many interacting factors</strong> (Boundary): Control rules, regulation practices and protection settings are part of the system, not only the power plants.</li>
<li><strong>gaps in voltage and reactive-power control</strong> (Physics): Voltage is held locally with reactive power; frequency is the system-wide balance of lesson 0. A voltage problem is not a shortage of energy.</li>
<li><strong>Left unanswered</strong> (Counterfactual): Compared with what? The headline skips the test: would the same plants with different control settings, or different plants with the same settings, have held? The panel's event-by-event analysis is how such questions get answered.</li>
<li><strong>A researcher's take</strong>: I reject the claim that renewables alone caused the blackout. An investigation tracing the collapse to one cause would change my mind. Confidence: high that there was no single cause, because the expert panel found many interacting factors.</li></ul></details>
<p class="lx-hint">Source: <a href="https://www.entsoe.eu/publications/blackout/28-april-2025-iberian-blackout/">ENTSO-E, 28 April 2025 Iberian blackout: expert panel reports</a> (factual report 3 October 2025; final report 20 March 2026)</p>
<!-- fallback:end -->
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you tag each story's phrases yourself, run a check with units, and compare with a researcher's notes.</p>
</div>
</div>
<p class="lx-datanote"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><span>Headlines are paraphrased in our own words; no outlet is quoted. Facts come from the primary sources linked in each story (LBNL via the U.S. Department of Energy, EIA, ENTSO-E), as of the dates shown, checked on 2 November 2026. Battery durations and connection use in the checks are illustrative.</span></p>
```

::: {#explain .lx-sec}

## What you just did, as a checklist and a ladder
:::

```{=html}
<div id="n1-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>The lens</dt><dd>Seven questions, always in the same order: scale, time, physics, who pays, boundary, counterfactual, uncertainty.</dd>
<dt>Power or energy</dt><dd><span class="lx-term" data-term="gigawatt">GW</span> is a rate and GWh an amount; dividing a year's TWh by 8,760 hours gives average GW.</dd>
<dt>The evidence ladder</dt><dd>Announced, funded, permitted, under construction, operating, at design output; a <span class="lx-term" data-term="projection">projection</span> is not on the ladder.</dd>
<dt>Your take</dt><dd>The claim you accept or reject, what would change your mind, and your confidence.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Three more checks for the next tier</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li><strong>Evidence status.</strong> Which rung of the ladder is the claim on? A plan, a permit and a running plant are different news.</li>
<li><strong>Jurisdiction and date.</strong> Rules belong to a place and a year; a tariff or credit that applies in one state, or before a rule change, may not apply elsewhere.</li>
<li><strong>Which emissions question?</strong> A share of a grid's emissions, the short-run change from adding a load, the long-run change through what gets built, and what a buyer may claim are four questions with four methods.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Steelman</span>Why the 2030 data-center projection could come out lower, or higher</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<p>The report's own sensitivity scenarios give the strongest case each way (LBNL 2025 Update, p. 5):</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Lower:</strong> fewer IT installations than forecast (578 TWh in 2030), or shorter working lives for specialised chips (590 TWh).</li>
<li><strong>Higher:</strong> more specialised graphics chips installed (664 TWh), or servers that draw more power when idle and run busier (782 TWh).</li>
</ul>
<p>Combined, the authors' bounds are 521–843 TWh. A careful reader reports the range and the drivers, not one number.</p>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Which model would test each claim?</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li><strong>Story 1:</strong> a planning model that adds the new load hour by hour and asks what must be built to serve it (upcoming: M3, capacity expansion).</li>
<li><strong>Story 2:</strong> a storage dispatch model, where the duration limits how long each battery can discharge (lesson 9 on the <a href="09-storage.html">course map</a>).</li>
<li><strong>Story 3:</strong> a power-flow and dynamics study of voltage and protection; the course shows when an energy-only answer fails (upcoming: A17) but stops short of dynamic simulation.</li>
</ul>
<p>Modeler's note: at the next tier the drill changes from "which question?" to "which model would test this, and what result would prove it wrong?"</p>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>The three stories were chosen because their primary sources are public and well documented; many headlines are harder to trace.</li>
<li>The lens tells you what to ask, not what is true. Answers come from data, models and investigations.</li>
<li>Numbers are dated. Estimates get revised, including past years.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

::: {#check .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="n1-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="gwh" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A fleet of 15 GW of batteries stores 15 GWh.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Only if every battery lasts exactly one hour: <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy">energy</span> is power times duration, and the duration is often missing from the story.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="range" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A <span class="lx-term" data-term="projection">projection</span>'s range guarantees that the true value will fall inside it.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A range comes from the scenarios its authors chose; reality can land outside it, and later reports revise past years too.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cause" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A blackout during hours of high renewable output proves that renewables caused it.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Timing is not cause. Investigations rebuild the sequence of events; the Iberian expert panel found many interacting factors.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="share" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If data centers use 4.7% of U.S. electricity, they use about 4.7% of the world's.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A share depends on the whole you divide by; a national share and a global share answer different questions.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="n1">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="year" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A 2 GW load runs at full power for a whole year. How much <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy">energy</span> is that?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">2 GWh</li><li data-value="b">17.5 TWh</li><li data-value="c">17,520 TWh</li><li data-value="d">2 TWh</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>17.5 TWh: 2 GW × 8,760 h = 17,520 GWh. GW is a rate; a year's amount is in GWh or TWh.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cf" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">A story says a policy saved money “compared with a year without it”. Which lens question is that phrase about?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Scale</li><li data-value="b">Boundary</li><li data-value="c">Counterfactual</li><li data-value="d">Uncertainty</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p><span class="lx-term" data-term="counterfactual">Counterfactual</span>: it names the baseline. Next, ask whether that baseline would really have happened.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
:::

<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/electricity-in-the-us-generation-capacity-and-sales.php">Electricity generation, capacity, and sales in the United States</a> (utility-scale means 1 MW or more) and <a href="https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/use-of-electricity.php">Use of electricity</a>. Energy Explained.</li>
<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=97&amp;t=3">How much electricity does an American home use?</a> Frequently Asked Questions (10,791 kWh a year, 2022 data).</li>
<li>ENTSO-E (2025, 2026). <a href="https://www.entsoe.eu/publications/blackout/28-april-2025-iberian-blackout/">28 April 2025 Iberian blackout</a>: the expert panel's factual report (3 October 2025) and final report (20 March 2026).</li>
</ul>
